Received April **, ****; accepted *** **, ****
Abstract

We present a spatially resolved study of cold molecular gas and dust in ten main-sequence galaxies at z=1.1−1.6z=1.1-1.6, using observations of CO(4-3), CO(3-2), [C i](1-0), and dust continuum from the NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} survey. We find a widely presence of spatially extended molecular gas and dust, with sizes comparable to those of the stellar disk, in contrast to those of central-dominated starburst galaxies at similar redshifts. While various molecular gas tracers generally exhibit similar spatial distributions, the CO line (J=3−2J=3-2 or J=4−3J=4-3) remain the most effective for mapping molecular gas distribution and kinematics. In addition, the spatially resolved correlations between different molecular gas tracers exhibit about two times larger scatter than their galactic-integrated correlations, indicating that interstellar medium (ISM) conditions already deviate from global averages on scales of 3–6 kpc, likely reflecting the clumpy or inhomogeneous ISM in cosmic noon star-forming galaxies. Within our sample, both the molecular gas fraction and its depletion time are nearly constant across the galactic disks out to 2×Re2\times R_{\text{e}}, supporting a global linear Kennicutt–Schmidt law. The presence of extended molecular gas disks, along with regular stellar structures, small central bulges, and ordered cold gas kinematics, supports the idea that the evolution of main-sequence disk galaxies at cosmic noon is driven by steady gas accretion and transport through prominent spiral arms and/or bars. This process stands in contrast to the merger-driven stochastic gas accretion in compact starbursts.

Key Words.
Main-sequence galaxies – Starburst galaxies – Interstellar medium –

1 Introduction

The epoch around z∼1−3z\sim 1-3, often dubbed “cosmic noon”, marks the peak of the cosmic star formation rate density (Madau and Dickinson, 2014). Star-forming galaxies (SFGs) at this epoch follow a tight sequence on the stellar mass versus star formation rate (SFR) plane (Noeske et al., 2007; Elbaz et al., 2007; Rodighiero et al., 2011; Sargent et al., 2012; Speagle et al., 2014; Schreiber et al., 2015, the main sequence, or MS;), which supports a global paradigm that regulates the evolution of star-forming galaxies. To remain on the MS, galaxies require a continuous replenishment of cold gas, which can either be fresh gas accreted from the cosmic web, gas-rich mergers, or recycled gas from previous star formation or AGN feedback (see Tacconi et al. 2020 for a review). Consequently, the net availability of cold gas, particularly molecular gas, regulates the rise and fall of star formation inside galaxies and is a key ingredient supporting the growth of galaxies (Tacconi et al., 2010; Daddi et al., 2010; Tacchella et al., 2016; Baker et al., 2022). Over the past decade, one of the major achievements in understanding the cosmic star formation history has been the measurements of the cosmic evolution of molecular gas density (Genzel et al., 2015; Scoville et al., 2016; Tacconi et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019; Tacconi et al., 2020; Péroux and Howk, 2020; Walter et al., 2020; Riechers et al., 2020; Boogaard et al., 2023; Bollo et al., 2025). Both the star formation rate density and molecular gas density peak at 1<z<31<z<3, underscoring the vital importance of molecular gas content in driving the global, secular evolution of galaxies. The next step forward is to resolve the spatial distribution, excitation conditions, and kinematics of the cold gas at cosmic noon, connecting the cold gas cycle with galactic structure formation, dynamics, and quenching mechanisms during this globally transitional period (Förster Schreiber and Wuyts, 2020; Genzel et al., 2023, e.g.).

However, spatially resolved information about the molecular gas content of star-forming galaxies remains incomplete, particularly during the peak epoch of cosmic star formation. Various tracers have been used to estimate the total molecular gas mass, including carbon monoxide (CO) in its many rotational transitions and isotopic lines, cold dust emission, and neutral carbon (Bolatto et al., 2013; Carilli and Walter, 2013; Tacconi et al., 2020, see reviews by). Despite uncertainties in the individual conversion factors for different tracers, global cross-comparisons indicate that they generally yield consistent results for integrated galactic measurements (Genzel et al., 2015; Scoville et al., 2016; Tacconi et al., 2018; Dunne et al., 2022). However, there have been few direct, resolved comparisons of different cold-gas tracers at cosmic noon, which cautions against their use for mapping the spatial distribution of molecular gas (Arriagada-Neira et al., 2025; Boogaard et al., 2026, e.g.).

In addition, our current understanding of the molecular gas distribution in star-forming galaxies is largely biased toward starbursting galaxies at cosmic noon and earlier cosmic epoches. Majority of the observed targets are submillimeter galaxies (SMGs) or dusty star-forming galaxies (DSFGs), which mostly lie above the MS (Casey et al., 2014; Hodge and da Cunha, 2020, see reviews by). Studies of these galaxies have reported compact dust morphology with sizes often several times smaller than that traced by CO and stellar emission (Hodge et al., 2015; Spilker et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2017; Calistro Rivera et al., 2018; Boogaard et al., 2026). Observations of less extreme but still massive star-forming galaxies (SFGs) have shown similar trends, albeit with smaller differences between the sizes of molecular lines, dust continuum, and stars (Tadaki et al., 2017; Tadaki et al., 2023; Kaasinen et al., 2020; Pantoni et al., 2021). Furthermore, owing to observational depth limitations, current data are strongly biased toward high-contrast, central starburst regions, leaving extended dust emission from stellar disks potentially buried in the noise (Cochrane et al., 2019; Kaasinen et al., 2020, e.g.,). These apparent size differences caution against the indiscriminate use of different tracers to map molecular gas distributions and underscore the need for systematic, resolved studies of a more representative sample.

Moreover, as the fuel of star formation, the spatially resolved distribution of cold molecular gas directly reflects ongoing stellar buildup and quenching processes. Large near-infrared integrated field unit (IFU) surveys have revealed that the majority of the massive MS galaxies at cosmic noon are rotation-dominated (Förster Schreiber and Wuyts, 2020, see review from), a picture further supported by the prominent spiral arms and bars observed in these systems (Guo et al., 2023; Le Conte et al., 2024; Espejo Salcedo et al., 2025, e.g.). Together, the current evidence suggests that the growth of these galaxies was likely fueled by smooth gas accretion and minor mergers, rather than disruptive major mergers. Importantly, kinematic studies have revealed large-scale, rapid gas inflows in such systems (Genzel et al., 2023), consistent with perturbations from early-established stellar structures such as galactic bars and spirals (Übler et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025; Pastras et al., 2025, Pulsoni et al. in prep.). The resolved molecular gas in these galaxies thus completes our picture of how gas transport shapes ongoing star formation. However, resolving the molecular gas distribution in typical MS galaxies at cosmic noon requires very sensitive observations. So far, this has been done for just a few cases, benefiting from fortuitous lensing magnification or rare, very deep on-source integration (Liu et al., 2023; Arriagada-Neira et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025).

To this aim, we designed and conducted the NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} survey to assemble a sizeable sample of massive MS SFGs at z∼1.1−1.6z\sim 1.1-1.6, enabling us to map the cold gas and dust emission on scales of a few kpc. NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} makes use of the IRAM Northern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA), the successor of the Plateau de Bure Interferometer (PdBI). NOEMA’s wide bandwidth enables it to simultaneously cover multiple spectral lines and achieve ultra-deep sensitivity in the dust continuum. Jolly et al. (2026) (hereafter Paper 1) investigated the kinematic properties of the sample and highlighted the prominent radial gas flows associated with spiral arms and bars. Pastras et al. (2025); Pastras et al. (2026) investigated the radial gas flows in two barred systems and compared them with high-resolution simulations. In this work, we focus on the spatial distribution of molecular gas and dust, and discuss how their distributions inform our understanding of the evolution of massive MS galaxies at cosmic noon.

In this paper, we first briefly introduce NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} in §2, focusing on the observational setup of different cold ISM tracers. This section also includes descriptions of the multi-wavelength ancillary data and the integrated and resolved galaxy properties derived from SED fitting. §3 covers the steps of data analysis, including size measurement, radial profiles of different galactic components, and molecular gas mass measurements. We discuss our results in §4, covering the size comparison of different components, comparison with literature results, mass-size evolution, and bulge growth. We then compare different molecular gas tracers, CO, [C i], and dust continuum in §5. Then, in §6, we discuss the implications of our results in the context of massive galaxy formation. Finally, §7 summarizes all of our key results. Throughout the paper, we adopt the Chabrier stellar initial mass function (Chabrier, 2003) and a flat Λ\LambdaCDM cosmology with H0 = 70 km s-1 and Ωm=0.3\Omega_{\text{m}}=0.3.

2 NOEMA3D and Ancillary Data

2.1 NOEMA3D

NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} is the first systematic deep survey of cold molecular gas in MS galaxies around cosmic noon. It target 10 massive MS galaxies between z=1.1−1.6z=1.1-1.6, pushing the spatial resolution down to sub-arcsecond scales (0.3–0.7"", or 3–6 kpc in physical resolution). It is featured with deep integration, 22–70 hours of on-source time, to probe the spatial distribution of cold molecular gas and its kinematics. The global properties of these galaxies have been summarized in Table. 1. We refer the reader to 75 for a full description of the sample selection and observation design, and here we only summarize the details most relevant to this paper.

The NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} targets were observed using a combination of the A and C configurations of NOEMA. The observations were conducted between 2019 and 2024 under optimal weather conditions in Band 2 or Band 3. For targets around z∼1.2z\sim 1.2, the receivers were configured to cover 12CO J=4−3J=4-3, hereafter CO(4–3), and [C i](P13−P03{}^{3}P_{1}-{}^{3}P_{0}), hereafter [C i](1-0), simultaneously. For targets at z∼1.5z\sim 1.5, the receivers were configured to cover 12CO J=3−2J=3-2, hereafter CO(3–2). For simplicity, we refer to the z∼1.2z\sim 1.2 targets covering CO(4–3) as group-1, and the z∼1.5z\sim 1.5 targets covering CO(3–2) as group-2. In addition to the spectral lines, we also utilized the full available bandwidth of 15.5 GHz to cover the continuum emission around 1.3 mm (group-1) and 2 mm (group-2). All data were calibrated with clic and imaged with mapping from the GILDAS package11 1 https://www.iram.fr/IRAMFR/GILDAS/.

In addition to the full datacube products as described in 75, we also produced line intensity images for this work. We first extracted the spectrum from the datacube to identify the line-emitting channels. The image of each emission line was then created by collapsing all line-emission channels in the u​vuv plane and cleaned with natural weighting to achieve the best available sensitivity and recovery of extended emission. The continuum image was created by collapsing all the line-free channels from both subbands. In the final image products, the CO image show a slightly larger beam size than [C i](1-0) and the continuum, due to its lower frequency. To facilitate spatial comparison and line ratios, we recreated the images of [C i](1-0) and continuum using the same CLEAN beam as the CO images. All images are shown in Fig. 1 and 2 for group-1 and group-2 targets, respectively.

2.2 Multi-wavelength ancillary data

2.2.1 HST and JWST photometry

We collected broadband images from various public HST and JWST surveys (see 75 for a complete list of program IDs). For JWST images, we first retrieved high-quality reduced data from the public DAWN JWST Archive (DJA22 2 https://dawn-cph.github.io/dja/) whenever available. For public data but not yet available on DJA, we downloaded the raw data from the MAST33 3 https://mast.stsci.edu/search/ database and performed our own reduction using a customized JWST pipeline 44 4 https://github.com/1054/Crab.Toolkit.JWST (see also Espejo Salcedo et al. 2025). The HST data include both ACS and WFC3/IR observations, covering wavelengths from the F435W to F160W bands (rest-frame in ≈0.17\approx 0.17–0.7 μ\mum). The JWST data consist of NIRCam and MIRI imaging, spanning the F090W–F2100W range (rest-frame in ≈0.4\approx 0.4–9 μ\mum).

Using the broadband images, we created color-composite images using the JWST/NIRCam and/or HST/ACS–WFC3 bands, assigning blue filters (<1​μ<1\penalty\ \mum) to the blue channel, red filters (>3​μ>3\penalty\ \mum) to the red channel, and intermediate filters to the green channel. Since the filter coverage varies from target to target, the exact combinations differ accordingly. For the only target without JWST coverage, G4-38065, the color image was produced using HST filters alone, assigning the reddest filters (>1​μ>1\penalty\ \mum) to red, the bluest filters (<0.5​μ<0.5\penalty\ \mum) to blue, and the remaining ones to green. The resulting color images are shown in Figs. 1 and 2.

2.2.2 Host galaxy properties

Table 1 lists the integrated properties of our sample. Here, we provide a brief summary of the photometric datasets and the main assumptions used to perform the SED fitting.

We used all publicly available photometry, with slightly different wavelength coverage depending on the data availability for each target (75, see Table A.1 in). In particular, we extracted integrated photometry from HST/ACS and WFC3/IR, and JWST/NIRCam, complemented by mid- and far-IR data from Spitzer/IRAC (3.6–8 μ\mum) and MIPS 24 μ\mum (Dickinson et al., 2003; Whitaker et al., 2014), and from Herschel/PACS (70–160 μ\mum; Lutz et al. 2011). In addition, we included integrated dust continuum measurements from our NOEMA observations in Band 3 (1.4 mm) and Band 2 (2 mm) (presented in Sect. 2.1).

Based on the multi-wavelength data, we performed integrated SED fitting with CIGALE (Boquien et al., 2019) to derive the main global physical properties of the galaxies, including stellar mass (M⋆M_{\star}), star formation rate (SFR), and far-IR (FIR) luminosity. For each galaxy, we fixed the redshift to the known spectroscopic value and assumed a constant star formation history (SFH, parameterized with exponentially declining SFH with an e-folding time τ=8000\tau=8000 Myr). We adopted the stellar population synthesis models of Bruzual and Charlot (2003), assumed a Chabrier (2003) initial mass function, fixed the metallicity to the Solar value (Z=0.02Z=0.02), and included the nebular emission module. Dust attenuation was modeled following Calzetti et al. (2000), while dust emission was reproduced using the templates of Dale et al. (2014). The stellar masses and FIR luminosity were taken directly from the CIGALE outputs, while the total SFRs were computed from the combination of UV and IR luminosity of the SED best-fit models, following the empirical relations of Kennicutt (1998).

In addition to the integrated quantities described above, we also make use of spatially resolved maps of stellar mass, SFR, and dust attenuation (AV{}_{\text{V}}) obtained from a spatially resolved SED fitting of HST/ACS and WFC3/IR, and JWST/NIRCam imaging. The pixel-by-pixel SED fitting was performed under the same assumptions adopted for the integrated SED analysis, after convolving all the available HST and JWST images to the spatial resolution of the JWST/NIRCam F444W band, or to that of the HST/WFC3 F160W band when JWST data were not available. Detailed spatially resolved SED fitting analysis will be presented in Tozzi et al. (in prep.).

3 Analysis

In this section, we present our methods to derive all the resolved quantities, including size measurements, radial profiles, and molecular gas mass.

3.1 Size measurements

3.1.1 Stars

To measure the intrinsic size of the stellar mass distribution, one needs to account for various observational effects, including the PSF smearing, dust attenuation, and the mass-to-light (M/L) ratio. JWST offers deep images with spatial resolution better than 0.2 arcsec, which is significantly smaller than the effective radius of our targets, typically larger than 0.5 arcsec. Meanwhile, JWST also probes the rest-frame near-IR emission of these galaxies, which is less affected by dust attenuation. To further reduce the bias introduced by the mass-to-light ratio, we use the stellar mass maps derived from the spatially resolved SED fitting (see §2.2.2).

Given the relatively rich substructures in the stellar images, we adopted the non-parametric curve-of-growth method to measure the effective radius. We applied the curve-of-growth method directly to the stellar mass maps to derive the fiducial stellar size. We first defined the extracting aperture based on the inclination and position angle of the galaxy derived from \al@ Jolly2026 (see also in Table. 3). Then, we gradually increased the aperture size to derive the curve-of-growth curve; the radius that includes half of the total mass is later defined as the effective radius along the major axis (Re, starR_{\text{e, star}}). One example of this method can be found in Fig. A. To compare with the literature results, we also derived the effective radius Re,500nmR_{\text{e,500nm}} and the size including 80% stellar emission R80,500nmR_{\text{80,500nm}} at the rest-frame optical wavelength (∼5000\sim 5000 Å), Across the paper, we quote the effective radius from the stellar mass as the reference size ReR_{\text{e}}. All the derived effective sizes are summarized in Table 2. Note that the projection effect from the intrinsic 3D galaxy morphology also affects the size measurements, but the effect is statistically small (van der Wel et al., 2023), especially for the disk-dominated galaxies discussed here.

3.1.2 Molecular lines and dust continuum

We used a different strategy to measure the sizes of the molecular gas and dust continuum with NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}}. First, the spatial resolution of NOEMA is lower than that of HST and JWST, making the PSF a dominant factor in size measurements. Because of this, we use parametric model with forward modeling to correct for PSF smearing. To approximate the intrinsic light distribution, we used a general 2D Sérsic profile, which is sufficiently flexible to model most of our data. Second, interferometric observations sample the Fourier space of projected sky images and use non-linear CLEAN algorithms to recover the sky images from the dirty images. The CLEANing process introduces correlated noise in the final image, and its gridding and weighting schemes come at the cost of averaging and downweighting part of the u​vuv data. There have been many discussions about the advantages of modeling in the u​vuv space, which benefits from improved noise behavior and maximal information recovery (Martí-Vidal et al., 2014; Spilker et al., 2016; Tazzari et al., 2018; Kurtovic and Pinilla, 2024, e.g.). Therefore, to better recover the intrinsic spatial extent of the cold gas and dust, we performed the 2D Sérsic fitting directly in the u​vuv plane. We first modeled the data from the CLEANed image to obtain initial model parameter. Then, we constructed the model and transformed it into visibility, from where we compare with observed visibility to perform χ2\chi^{2} minimization. Depending on the integrated SNR of the data, we occasionally need to fix some parameters, such as disk ellipticity and Sérsic index, to achieve convergence in the fitting. The best-fit models and final residuals are shown in Figs. 15–17. All best-fit parameters are summarized in Table 4, while derived major-axis effective radius in kpc is summarized in Table 2.

For the final size comparison, we adopt the CO size measurement as the reference for the molecular gas size in group-1. The reasons are: 1) we generally find comparable size measurements between CO(4–3) and [C i] under the assumption of an intrinsic Sérsic profile (see Table 4); 2) CO(4–3) is brighter than [C i], providing more robust measurements without requiring additional fixed parameters. However, future follow-up observations covering additional CO and [C i] transitions are required to derive their excitation conditions and optical depth.

Dust size measurements are known to be influenced by optical depth and dust temperature distributions. With NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}}, the unprecedented continuum sensitivity allows probing the fully resolved dust emission at the ∼\sim1.4 mm (group-1, rest-frame ∼650​μ\sim 650\,\mum) and 2 mm (group-2, rest-frame ∼800​μ\sim 800\,\mum). At these wavelengths, dust emission is largely optically thin and proportional to the distribution of the total dust mass (Scoville et al., 2016), which is also less sensitive to the radial temperature variations. Due to the unknown dust temperature gradients, we still used the constant-temperature assumption, which likely underestimates the extent of the intrinsic dust size (Cochrane et al., 2019; Mitsuhashi et al., 2024, see also). However, the typical error introduced is small, within 0.2 dex (see more detailed discussion in Appendix B).

3.2 Bulge–disk decomposition

Most of our galaxies exhibit prominent central stellar light concentration in the rest-frame near-IR, resembling the bulge component widely seen in nearby galaxies. For simplicity, we will continue to refer to these features as “bulges”, with the caveat that they may not fully correspond to the classical spherical bulge component observed in more nearby systems, as we will discuss later.

We performed bulge–disk decomposition using two 2D Sérsic profiles to characterize the bulge profile and quantify the bulge-to-total ratio (B/T). While the extended stellar disk is not strongly affected by smearing, the compact central bulge lies largely within the PSF and thus requires forward modelling that accounts for PSF smearing. We modeled the bulge as a spheroid with its axis ratio fixed to 1. To reduce degeneracy between the two Sérsic components and better separate the bulge contribution, we apply the following constrains to our model before the global fitting. We first tied the centers of the bulge and the disk together. We then derived the center of the bulge by fitting only the central 2 kpc region, which is later fixed during the global fitting. For the disk component, we adopted its position angle and inclination from a joint analysis of isophote fitting and the kinematics (75, see more details in). We also restricted our modeling to the reddest available filters (F444W and F160W for G4-38065) to minimize dust attenuation. During fitting, the combined disk and bulge model is convolved with the model PSF, which is constructed using the Space Telescope PSF (STPSF) toolkit55 5 https://stpsf.readthedocs.io and stacked in the same manner as the science data from different exposures (Pastras et al., 2026). The fitting is done in two iterations. The first fitting uses differential evolution algorithm to search a wide parameter space and calculate the initial guess for the second least-squares minimization. The best-fit parameters are summarized in Table 3. The images, along with the best-fit models and residuals, are shown in Fig. 3.

Even with all these constraints, the fitting sometimes fails to converge on the bulge component. In such cases, we fixed the Sérsic index nn of the bulge component to 1. There are two main reasons that led us to select a lower Sérsic index, rather than the widely adopted value of n=4n=4 (Tacchella et al., 2015, e.g.). First, based on the results of successful fits, the Sérsic indices are typically much lower than 4. Second, we tested a grid of Sérsic indices for the bulge and found that n=1n=1 consistently provides a better fit than larger Sérsic indices. The implications of such bulge components are discussed in §4.3. Four galaxies in our sample also show a prominent galactic bar; in those cases, we fixed both the Sérsic index of the bulge (n=2n=2) and the disk (n=1n=1) to avoid bias from the bar component.

3.3 Flux density profiles

We averaged the data within radial elliptical annuli to construct the radial profiles of different cold gas tracers and stars. To ensure consistent comparison between the observables, we first convolved the stellar emission down to the same resolution as the CO images. Here we mainly compared with the stellar profile from JWST/NIRCam F444W (HST/WFC3 F160W for G4-38065), which provides the closest approximation of the stellar mass profile (see example in Fig. 13). We did not use the resolved SED map here to keep the comparison to observables only. To achieve uniform sampling across different components, we first fit a 2D Sérsic profile to the resolution-degraded stellar images to determine the axis ratio of the extracting aperture, which were then used to all other components. The derived radial profiles of CO(3-2), CO(4-3), [C i](1-0), dust, and stars are shown in Fig. 4.

In general, we found that most galaxies show consistent radial profiles across different components, with differences largely within their 1​σ1\penalty\ \sigma variations. However, not all the cold ISM tracers follow the same radial profiles. In G4-38065 and G4-38232, we observed more extended dust emission, mainly driven by off-center dust emission. Overall, such global similarity in radial profiles is significantly different from what has been observed in more extreme dusty star-forming galaxies, where the dust is found to be more compact than the gas and stars (Hodge et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2017; Calistro Rivera et al., 2018).

3.4 Molecular gas mass

In this sub-section, we discuss various scaling relations used to estimate the molecular gas mass for our observations. The group-1 targets provide us with the opportunity to compare three tracers simultaneously, namely CO(4-3), [C i](1-0) and the dust continuuum, and assess the potential impact of variations in excitation/dust temperature on the global molecular gas estimates. We mostly only have CO(3-2) for the group-2 targets, which is a reliable molecular gas tracer for massive main-sequence galaxies (Tacconi et al., 2020). We used the empirical calibration derived directly from CO(1-0) whenever possible to avoid any cross-calibration issues between different tracers. The molecular gas mass, MmolM_{\text{mol}}, represents the total molecular gas mass, including the 36 percent mass contribution from helium.

3.4.1 CO

Studies of the CO SLED have been conducted in numerous star-forming galaxies around cosmic noon. However, due to the faintness of CO(1-0), direct calibration compared to CO(1-0) is very limited (Aravena et al., 2010; Aravena et al., 2014; Bolatto et al., 2015; Henríquez-Brocal et al., 2022; Frias Castillo et al., 2023; Prajapati et al., 2026, e.g.). In this study, we adopted the calibration proposed by Tacconi et al. (2020), who carefully compiled various literature data, homogenized the analysis, and conducted convergence tests (Genzel et al., 2015; Tacconi et al., 2018, see also). We then estimated the molecular gas mass with the following equations:

LCO′=3.25×107​SCO​Δ​\varv​vobs−2​DL2​(1+z)−3​K km s−1​pc2Mmol=αCO×R1J×LCOJ-(J-1)′​M⊙\begin{split}&L^{\prime}_{\text{CO}}=3.25\times 10^{7}\,S_{\text{CO}}\,\Delta\varv\,v_{\text{obs}}^{-2}D_{\text{L}}^{2}(1+z)^{-3}\,\,\text{K\,km\,s}^{-1}\text{pc}^{2}\\ &M_{\text{mol}}=\alpha_{\text{CO}}\times R_{\text{1J}}\times L^{\prime}_{\text{CO}_{\text{J-(J-1)}}}\,\,\text{M}_{\odot}\end{split} (1)

Here, SCO​Δ​\varvS_{\text{CO}}\Delta\varv is measured in Jy km s-1; the observed frequency vobsv_{\text{obs}} is in GHz; and the luminosity distance DLD_{\text{L}} is in Mpc. Following Tacconi et al. (2020), we adopted the recommended αCO=4.36±0.9\alpha_{\text{CO}}=4.36\pm 0.9 M⊙\text{M}_{\odot} K km s-1 pc2, and a CO ladder correlation of R14=2.4R_{14}=2.4 and R13=1.8R_{13}=1.8 for group-1 and group-2 targets, respectively.

3.4.2 Dust Continuum

Long-wavelength dust emission has gained popularity as an alternative method for measuring molecular gas mass (Eales et al., 2012; Magdis et al., 2012; Scoville et al., 2014, e.g.). At millimeter wavelengths, dust emission is primarily optically thin, with the observed flux being proportional to its mass (Scoville et al., 2014; Scoville et al., 2016; Scoville et al., 2017). Our observations were mostly conducted around restframe 650 μ\mum and 800μ\mum; thus, we can safely use these measurements to trace the distribution of molecular gas mass. We adopted the conversion from Scoville et al. (2016), which has been empirically calibrated using a sample of star-forming galaxies with CO(1-0) observations at various redshifts, star formation rates, stellar masses, and spanning three orders of magnitude in dust emission.

Lv850​μ​m=4​π​Svobs×K⁡(DL21+z)​W Hz−1K=(353​G​H​zvrest)3+β​(eh​vrest/k/Td−1e16.956/Td−1)Mmol=Lv850​μ​mαv850​μ​m​M⊙\begin{split}&L_{v_{\rm 850\mu m}}=4\pi\,S_{v_{\text{obs}}}\times K\,\left(\frac{D^{2}_{\text{L}}}{1+z}\right)\,\,\text{W Hz}^{-1}\\ &K=\left(\frac{\rm 353GHz}{v_{\text{rest}}}\right)^{3+\beta}\left(\frac{e^{\text{h}v_{\text{rest}}/k/T_{\text{d}}}-1}{e^{16.956/T_{\text{d}}}-1}\right)\\ &M_{\text{mol}}=\frac{L_{v_{\rm 850\mu m}}}{\alpha_{v_{\rm 850\mu m}}}\,\,\text{M}_{\odot}\end{split} (2)

Here, KK is the K-correction between the observed frequency and 850μ\mum. We adopted Td=25T_{\text{d}}=25 K, β=1.8\beta=1.8, and αv850​μ​m=6.7±1.7×1012​W Hz−1​M⊙−1\alpha_{v_{\rm 850\mu m}}=6.7\pm 1.7\times 10^{12}\text{W\,Hz}^{-1}\text{M}_{\odot}^{-1}, as recommended by Scoville et al. (2016). It is noteworthy that the 25 K dust temperature is a mass-weighted average, since most dust in the ISM is supposed to be cold. Scoville et al. (2016) cautioned against using a variable dust temperature in the scaling relation for converting dust continuum to total molecular gas. This is because the observed dust SED is biased towards the luminosity-weighted dust temperature, which is influenced by the high temperatures of luminous star-forming regions. In contrast, mass-weighted dust is dominated by the more extended cloud envelopes, which remain less variable across galaxies.

3.4.3 CI

[C i](1-0) is sometimes considered as an alternative molecular gas mass tracer to CO(1-0) (Walter et al., 2011; Alaghband-Zadeh et al., 2013; Bothwell et al., 2017; Valentino et al., 2018; Valentino et al., 2020b; Bourne et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2021; Arriagada-Neira et al., 2025). It has a low excitation temperature of about 24 K and a critical density similar to that of CO(1-0). Additionally, it has been found to correlate well with CO(1-0) in resolved nearby galaxies (Jiao et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2023). Its notable advantage lies in its better availability for z>1z>1 star-forming galaxies, where CO(1-0) becomes significantly harder to detect and resolve (Papadopoulos et al., 2004). Among its two commonly observed lines, [C i](1-0) is regarded as more reliable than [C i](2-1), as the latter can be strongly sub-thermally excited (Harrington et al., 2021; Papadopoulos et al., 2022). Based on an empirical analysis of the three most commonly used molecular gas tracers, Dunne et al. (2022) demonstrated that [C i](1-0) exhibits the least intrinsic scatter in the parameter space we are probing.

Following Dunne et al. (2022), we estimate the molecular mass from [C i](1-0) using:

LCI′=3.25×107​SCI​Δ​\varv​vobs−2​DL2​(1+z)−3​K km s−1​pc2Mmol=αCI​LCI′​M⊙\begin{split}&L^{\prime}_{\text{CI}}=3.25\times 10^{7}\,S_{\text{CI}}\,\Delta\varv\,v_{\text{obs}}^{-2}D_{\text{L}}^{2}(1+z)^{-3}\,\,\text{K\,km\,s}^{-1}\text{pc}^{2}\\ &M_{\text{mol}}=\alpha_{\text{CI}}L^{\prime}_{\text{CI}}\,\,\text{M}_{\odot}\end{split} (3)

Here, DLD_{L} is the luminosity distance in Mpc, and SCI​Δ​\varvS_{\text{CI}}\Delta\varv is the flux density of [C i](1-0) in Jy km s-1. We adopted the best-fit αCI=18.7±0.6\alpha_{\text{CI}}=18.7\pm 0.6, derived from direct minimization with a CO(1-0) sample of main-sequence galaxies reported by Dunne et al. (2022).

In summary, at an integrated level, all three molecular gas tracers return gas masses in reasonable agreement. However, as suggested by Tacconi et al. (2020), a fair comparison can only be made after properly correcting for zero-point offsets between methods. In this work, we have adopted separate sources of scaling relations that were calibrated largely independently, allowing the differences or offsets from each individual tracer to be better revealed.

4 Results

In this section, we discuss the evolutionary patterns of NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} galaxies, based on the physical properties derived and presented in §3.

4.1 Comparable size between gas, dust and stars

In Fig. 5, we compare all available size measurements from different components for NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} targets. We find broadly comparable sizes among stars, molecular gas, and dust, consistent with previous findings for MS galaxies (Tacconi et al., 2013; Tadaki et al., 2017; Puglisi et al., 2019; Kaasinen et al., 2020; Tadaki et al., 2023, e.g.). In our sample, all CO(4–3) emission appears centrally peaked. In G4-38232, the [C i] and dust continuum do not follow this general central-peaked distribution. In this case, the Sérsic profile failed to fit the observations. Given that the SNR for [C i](1-0) and dust are below ∼3​σ\sim 3\sigma, we did not include it in subsequent size comparisons. The same selection applies to most group-2 targets (3 of 4), for which we do not reliably detect dust emission.

We also compared the NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} targets with other galaxy types and simulations in Fig. 5. We included more starbursting SMGs (Chen et al., 2017; Calistro Rivera et al., 2018; Pantoni et al., 2021; Smail et al., 2023; Hodge et al., 2025), which generally show smaller dust and stellar sizes compared to molecular gas. Cochrane et al. (2019) conducted detailed radiative transfer simulations within the Feedback In Realistic Environments 2 (FIRE-2) framework, reproducing the relationship between dust and molecular gas sizes for both MS galaxies and starbursting SMGs. However, these FIRE-2 galaxies exhibit systematically smaller stellar sizes, likely due to the strong feedback models implemented in the simulations.

With the large availability of dust measurements for high-zz star-forming galaxies, we also show in Fig. 6 the correlation between FIR luminosity and dust size for different galaxy types across a broader cosmic history. We include the most extreme starbursting galaxies, SMGs, from a recent survey by Gullberg et al. (2019) at redshifts z=2z=2–4. We also incorporate a large sample of DSFGs from Tadaki et al. (2020), which includes SFGs mostly sit between MS galaxies and SMGs. To expand the sample of MS galaxies, we also include size measurements from the CRISTAL survey at z∼\sim5 (Mitsuhashi et al., 2024). Although available dust-size and FIR-luminosity measurements for MS galaxies are fewer by more than an order of magnitude than for SMGs, the intrinsic number density of MS galaxies is more than a magnitude higher (Chen et al., 2022, e.g.). Thus, the current samples are significantly biased toward brighter SMGs.

It is clear that MS galaxies and SMGs occupy distinct regions in the luminosity–size diagram. Starbursting SMGs are brighter in FIR emission due to their elevated star formation rates, which is concentrated in the centeral starburst core (<<1 kpc in size), resulting in an extreme average star-formation rate surface density, ∼1000​M⊙​kpc−2\sim 1000\,\text{M}_{\odot}\,\text{kpc}^{-2}. MS galaxies exhibit star formation rates about 1–2 orders of magnitude lower and are more extended, leading to a much lower average star-formation rate surface density. Even at much higher redshifts, MS galaxies from CRISTAL show a similar star-formation rate surface density. The CRISTAL galaxies show slightly smaller disks, but also have lower stellar masses and SFRs, keeping their surface density comparable to that of MS galaxies at cosmic noon.

We have also compared the two-dimensional (2D) morphology of the different molecular gas tracers in Appendix D. The CO generally exhibits larger asymmetries than [C i](1-0) and dust, likely due to its higher signal-to-noise ratio (S/N) at large radii. Because of the limited S/N in the [C i](1-0) and dust continuum data, we focus primarily on the radial profiles in the following discussion.

4.2 Size evolution

The mass-size evolution is one of the most fundamental tests for galaxy formation theories. Early studies based on HST have revealed two distinct populations: red quenched galaxies and blue star-forming galaxies, each following distinct mass-size relations (Toft et al., 2007; van der Wel et al., 2014). When we place our galaxies on the mass-size relation of cosmic noon galaxies (see Fig. 7), they align with the blue sequence and preferentially probe larger disks by the design of our selection. The fact that our galaxies reside within the blue sequence and exhibit prominent disk structures supports the notion that the growth in size and mass is primarily driven by in-situ star formation.

In the R80−M⋆R_{80}-M_{\star} relation, the NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} galaxies predominantly occupy the region around the transitional mass where the change in size becomes steeper (see Fig. 7). The stellar mass at this turning point corresponds to the stellar mass at the peak of the stellar-to-halo mass relation (SHMR) (Mowla et al., 2019), indicating that their halo masses are generally ∼25\sim 25 times their total stellar mass (Leauthaud et al., 2012). This provides an estimate for the total halo mass of our targets, in the range of 0.8−6×1012​M⊙0.8-6\times 10^{12}\text{M}_{\odot}. At z∼\sim1-1.5, these halos are approximately at the boundary where cold gas accretion remains feasible, a topic we will explore further in §6.1.

The environment can play a key role in the evolution of galaxy sizes. In dense environments, gas stripping due to tidal interactions and ram pressure can alter the spatial distribution of cold gas, ultimately affecting the overall growth of galaxies (Cortese et al., 2021). The NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} galaxies were selected specifically to avoid any close neighbours. From the most recent deep JWST images, none of them is undergoing an appreciable gravitational interaction with neighbouring galaxies. Their overall smooth morphology and regular kinematics (75) indicate that they are typically isolated disk galaxies. Moreover, environmental analysis of the CANDELS fields (Chartab et al., 2020) allows us to define the density contrast of each region based on the environmental overdensity δ=σ/σ¯−1\delta=\sigma/\bar{\sigma}-1. Here, σ¯\bar{\sigma} represents the background number density, while σ\sigma is the number density of target galaxies within a volume of 1​h−31h^{-3}Mpc3; thus, δ=0\delta=0 indicates no overdensity. According to this definition, the NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} galaxies are predominantly (8 out of 10) located in regions with density contrasts δ∼[−0.03,0.6]\delta\sim[-0.03,0.6], close to the mean density of main-sequence galaxies at cosmic noon. Galaxies G4-17555 and G4-24078 are situated in slightly denser regions with σ=1.2\sigma=1.2 and σ=1.7\sigma=1.7, respectively, but these values remain lower than the typical density contrasts found in (proto-)clusters at cosmic noon, where δ>2\delta>2 (Overzier, 2016, e.g.). Therefore, we do not expect significant environmental effects on the NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} galaxies.

4.3 Sub-dominant but ongoing formation of galactic bulge

The formation of bulges has been recognized as a key factor in modulating global star formation, particularly in explaining the bimodality observed in galaxy populations (Drory and Fisher, 2007; Bluck et al., 2014). In NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} galaxies, the bulge stands out only in the rest-frame near-infrared, as illustrated in Figs. 1 and 2 by their reddish color. Similar color gradients, where the central regions are redder than the outskirts, have been widely observed in star-forming galaxies at cosmic noon (Wuyts et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017a; Miller et al., 2022). Such color gradient could arise from variations in dust attenuation and/or stellar age. To quantify the effect of the dust on the central bulge, we investigated the correlation between dust mass density and SED-based attenuation in the NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} galaxies. We first derived the dust mass column density profile assuming that the rest-frame 650–800 μ\mum is mainly associated with the optically thin cold dust component with Td=25T_{\text{d}}=25 K, β=1.8\beta=1.8. The mass profiles in Fig. 8 support the idea that most dust is mainly cumulated in the galactic center. Meanwhile, we extracted the dust attenuation from the spatially resolved SED fitting and showed the correlation between dust mass column density and the SED-based dust attenuation at different galactic radii in Fig. 8. The measured Av range from 1 to ∼\sim3 in the rest-frame V band and show a typical attenuation of about 0.5−10.5-1 magnitudes higher within 0.5 ReR_{\text{e}} than in the outer disk. This confirms that the dust in these star-forming galaxies actively contributes to the color gradient and underscores the importance of correcting dust attenuation to recover the full picture of star formation in the central bulge. We also compared our measurements with the simplified screen and mixed models from Kreckel et al. (2013) and the hydrodynamic simulation incorporating full Monte Carlo radiative transfer from Trayford et al. (2020). Our measurements lie between the two simplified theoretical models, consistent with the behavior observed in nearby star-forming galaxies (Kreckel et al., 2013). Compared to the simulations, our measurements reveal stronger dust attenuation in the central regions, indicating a more pronounced dust-screening effect than currently implemented in the models.

The bulge components appear ubiquitous in the NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} sample, but the stellar mass in the bulge does not dominate the host galaxy. Our findings indicate that the stellar mass fraction of the central bulge typically constitutes 10 to 20 percent of the total stellar mass. Although the bulge Sérsic index cannot be robustly constrained from the current JWST images, our tests do favour a less peaked (Sérsic index n<3n<3) central bulge compared to classical bulges. Such a low Sérsic index is closer to the argument for a compact nuclear disk in the centers of galaxies (Gadotti, 2026; Le Conte et al., 2026). We also calculate the central stellar density within the inner 1 kpc region, denoted as Σ1​k​p​c\Sigma_{\rm 1kpc}, which ranges between 2−5×109​M⊙​kpc−22-5\times 10^{9}\,\text{M}_{\odot}\text{kpc}^{-2}. Given the stellar masses of NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} galaxies, the Σ1​k​p​c\Sigma_{\rm 1kpc} values approach the densities of typical compact quenched galaxies at similar redshifts (Barro et al., 2017), as illustrated in Fig. 7. However, unlike compact quenched systems, NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} galaxies still exhibit active star formation and large molecular gas reservoirs in their centers. Based on their morphologies and kinematics, we have ruled out major mergers as the trigger of their star formation, leaving secular growth as the primary channel to support bulge growth. Therefore, our observations suggest these massive disk galaxies at cosmic noon have not yet developed a full-fledged bulge component, and it is very likely that we are witnessing the ongoing formation of central bulges alongside the secular growth of galaxies (Genzel et al., 2008).

5 Comparison of molecular gas tracers

5.1 The spatially resolved flux correlations

We begin our comparison by breaking down the integrated luminosity correlation into resolved correlations with our group-1 targets. Figure 9 illustrates the one-to-one correlation between dust, CO(4-3), and [C i](1-0), for both the integrated and resolved measurements. To facilitate comparisons with the literature, we converted our measurements to the more commonly used reference. For instance, following the convention of Scoville et al. (2016), we converted the dust luminosity to 850 μ\mum using the K-correction computed from a modified blackbody with a dust temperature of 25 K and a dust emissivity of 1.8. The overall correction factor for the group-1 galaxies is approximately 0.5±0.10.5\pm 0.1, which does not significantly affect the measurements discussed here. In accordance with the recommendations of Tacconi et al. (2020), we adopted a global correction factor of 2.4 to convert CO(4-3) to CO(1-0). We also compared our results with the global correlations derived by Dunne et al. (2022), who compiled the largest current sample of galaxies with CO, [C i](1-0), and dust emissions.

Unsurprisingly, the integrated measurements align well with the correlations derived from the literature. Of particular interest is the consistency observed between CO(4-3) and [C i](1-0), which correlates nicely with the relationships derived from CO(1-0) and CO(2-1). This suggests that the global CO SLED correction of 2.4 performs reasonably well for these massive main-sequence galaxies (Tacconi et al., 2020, see also). By comparison, the resolved correlations display nearly two times larger scatter, indicating that different molecular gas tracers begin to behave differently on 3–6 kpc scales in massive star-forming galaxies. The increased scatter likely reflects the inhomogeneous ISM conditions on these scales, which could be rooted in the generally clumpy structure observed on similar or smaller scales (Förster Schreiber et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2012; Claeyssens et al., 2023; Kalita et al., 2025), or due to the widespread presence of radial gas flows in these gas-rich star-forming galaxies (Genzel et al., 2023; Pastras et al., 2025; Übler et al., 2024).

5.2 The line flux ratios

To further understand the behavior of different gas tracers as a function of galactic radius, we extracted radial profiles of their flux ratios, as illustrated in Fig. 10. These ratios were derived from the radial profiles of each tracer, sampled at intervals equal to half the beam size. A flux ratio was computed only when both tracers were detected with a significance greater than 3​σ3\sigma after integrating the signal within each radial annulus. For our comparison, we used the flux densities directly since all three tracers were observed at similar frequencies. The conversion from flux ratio to luminosity ratio requires only a correction for their frequency differences, which is on the order of ∼1.1\sim 1.1 and is generally smaller than their error bars.

Among the flux ratios, CO(4-3)/dust shows the flattest distribution. In theory, both CO(4-3)/dust and [C i](1-0)/dust can be considered first approximations of the gas-to-dust ratio. However, in star-forming regions, CO(4–3) (Text∼55T_{\text{ext}}\sim 55 K, ncrit∼2×104​cm−3n_{\text{crit}}\sim 2\times 10^{4}\,\text{cm}^{-3}) has nearly two times higher excitation temperature and a order of magnitude higher critical density than [C i](1-0) (Text∼24T_{\text{ext}}\sim 24 K, ncrit∼5×102​cm−2n_{\text{crit}}\sim 5\times 10^{2}\,\text{cm}^{-2}). Thus, CO(4-3)/dust is more representative of the gas-to-dust ratio in denser gas than CI(1-0)/dust. The nearly flat CO(4-3)/dust ratio in our sample indicates that CO(4-3) and the dust continuum around rest-frame 650​μ650\mum trace similar gas clouds within each galaxy, consistent with simulations by Cochrane et al. (2019). However, the absolute differences between individual galaxies are on the order of ∼0.6\sim 0.6 dex. The [C i](1-0)/dust ratio exhibits a larger radial variation in several galaxies compared to CO(4-3)/dust, likely due to their lower signal to noise ratios (S/N). The physical drivers behind these variations remain unclear. While metallicity has been implicated in the substantial variations of gas-to-dust ratios in nearby resolved galaxies (Leroy et al., 2011, e.g.), it is unlikely to hold for the NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} galaxies given their high stellar mass, especially considering that most resolved studies favored rather flat metallicity gradient among massive star-forming galaxies (Wang et al., 2017b; Wuyts et al., 2016; Förster Schreiber et al., 2018; Ju et al., 2025; Fujimoto et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026, e.g.). Another more likely reason could be the different excitation mechanisms of CO(4-3) and [C i](1-0) at various radii, as both the CO SLED and CI(2-1)/CI(1-0) ratios have been found to vary significantly with radiation fields and gas densities (Papadopoulos et al., 2012; Narayanan and Krumholz, 2014; Valentino et al., 2020b; Boogaard et al., 2020). Such spatially resolved excitation variations have already been observed in main-sequence galaxies at cosmic noon (Daddi et al., 2015, e.g.).

In Fig. 10, CO(4-3)/[C i](1-0) ratio shows quite some scatter with no clear variation trend across the radii. Due to their different critical densities, CO(4-3)/[C i](1-0) serves as a first-order approximation for the dense-to-total molecular gas ratio (Geach and Papadopoulos, 2012; Papadopoulos and Geach, 2012). The radial variations in the NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} targets can thus be attributed to changes in the relative abundance of dense versus diffuse molecular gas, which explains well the decreasing trends found in galaxies like GN4_18574 and G4_23011. Other galaxies, such as G4_38065 and GN4_24517, show a rather flat profile, which could indicate that the dense star-forming clouds also extend out to the outer disk. Integrated CO(4-3)/[C i](1-0) ratios have been widely observed to vary among different star-forming galaxies (Valentino et al., 2020b), with relatively high values (>>3) in extreme ULIRGs and lower values of ∼\sim1 in nearby star-forming disk galaxies. The ratio in the central (<Re<\!R_{\text{e}}) region of all galaxies is largely consistent with the integrated ratios of main-sequence galaxies at cosmic noon, although exhibiting a variation of about 0.3 dex. We also present the radial profile derived from BX610 (Arriagada-Neira et al., 2025, see Fig. 10), another main-sequence galaxy at z∼2.2z\sim 2.2. BX610’s central region shows a line ratio similar to that of ULIRGs, likely driven by an enhanced SFR fueled by efficient gas inflow (Genzel et al., 2023). Theoretically, an enhancement of [C i](1-0) could also suggest a deficit of CO due to the cosmic ray (CR) induced CO destruction in molecular clouds (Papadopoulos, 2010; Bisbas et al., 2015). We did not observe any significant decrease in the line ratios at the centers of our NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} targets, possibly canceled out by the brighter CO(4–3) emission due to the higher excitation temperature.

5.3 Spatially resolved gas fraction and depletion timescale

With the availability of spatially resolved stellar mass, SFR, and molecular gas mass, we can derive the spatially resolved molecular gas fraction (μmol=Mmol/M⋆\mu_{\text{mol}}=M_{\text{mol}}/M_{\star}) and gas depletion timescale (tdep=Mmol/SFRt_{\text{dep}}=M_{\text{mol}}/\text{SFR}). The integrated molecular gas fraction and depletion timescale of galaxies have been the subject of extensive discussion over the past decades (Genzel et al., 2015; Scoville et al., 2017; Tacconi et al., 2018, e.g.). Both quantities are found to show a strong dependence on redshift and on their relative distance from the spine of MS. The spatially resolved depletion timescales and molecular gas fractions provides a new perspective for quantifying their significance in a galaxy’s internal evolution.

We first examined the averaged radial profile of molecular gas fraction in our galaxies, as it could reveal the effects of bulges and disks. To account for the dependence of molecular gas fraction on stellar mass and redshift, we normalized the molecular gas fraction to that of MS galaxies with the same stellar mass and redshift, using the best-fit function of Tacconi et al. (2020). The radial profiles of the normalized molecular gas fraction are shown in Fig. 11 (see also the full results for different tracers in Fig. 19). Most galaxies exhibit only a slight increase or decrease in molecular gas fraction with radius, well within the measurement uncertainties. However, variations between galaxies are more significant, even after correcting for the effects of stellar mass and redshift. Galaxies are dynamic systems, which are thought to wander up and down during their different evolutional stage. The observed galaxy-to-galaxy variations are likely due to their different evolutionary stages relative to the main sequence. The sample-averaged molecular gas fraction in different ReR_{\text{e}} bins, shown as gray stars in Fig. 11, also favors a nearly flat trend out to 2×Re2\times R_{\text{e}} across our sample.

We also derived the radial profile of molecular gas depletion timescale, which reflects how long the currently available molecular gas can sustain the current SFR. Its inverse is also widely referred to as star formation efficiency. Similar to the molecular gas fraction, we also corrected for the dependence on stellar mass and redshift using the scaling relation for MS galaxies from Tacconi et al. (2020). In Fig. 11, most of our galaxies also exhibit a relatively flat profile in molecular gas depletion timescale. Such similar depletion timescales indicating star formation at different radii generally follow a similar Kennicutt–Schmidt law, similar to what has been found in the nearby Universe (Bigiel et al., 2011; Muraoka et al., 2019). The sample-averaged depletion timescale also favors a general flat trend, similar to that of the molecular gas fraction.

5.4 The optimal molecular gas tracers

CO, including the CO(4–3) and CO(3–2) transitions, remains the brightest tracer compared to [C i](1-0) and dust continuum within our observing setups, and it has been consistently detected for all of the NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} targets. It is well known that typical main-sequence (MS) galaxies exhibit a diverse CO spectral line energy distribution (SLED) (Daddi et al., 2015; Valentino et al., 2020a; Boogaard et al., 2020), which advises caution when using CO(4–3) alone as a tracer of total molecular gas mass. Nevertheless, overall our results support that CO(4–3) remains a reliable molecular gas tracer in typical MS galaxies at cosmic noon. Given its brightness in particular, it also serves as a powerful tracer for studying molecular gas kinematics (75).

[C i](1-0) has been widely proposed as an alternative to CO(1-0) (Papadopoulos et al., 2004; Prajapati et al., 2026, e.g.). Our results generally support that [C i](1-0) traces CO(4-3) fairly well on galactic scales of a few kpc, but their ratio show a modest galaxy-to-galaxy variation. Based on our observations alone, we cannot provide a definitive verdict on the reliability of [C i](1-0) in tracing the total molecular gas mass. However, a drawback to [C i](1-0) is that it is typically two times weaker than CO(4-3), requiring significantly longer telescope time to spatially resolve [C i](1-0), especially for studies focusing on the kinematics or dynamics of molecular gas.

Dust is generally faint in our observations. Within the group-1 targets, the dust continuum surface brightness is approximately 7–18 times fainter than that of CO(4–3) around rest-frame 650 μ\mum. The dust continuum is even fainter compared to CO(3–2) at rest-frame 800 μ\mum; among the group-2 targets, only GN4-32842 shows a clear detection of dust emission. The successful detection of dust continuum in NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} galaxies clearly demonstrates the powerful wideband capability of NOEMA, where the 15.5 GHz bandwidth compensates for a sensitivity about 6 times higher than that for the spectral line. Moreover, the intrinsic brightness of dust emission scales approximately with ν2\nu^{2} in the Rayleigh–Jeans tail, so observations at higher frequencies could also benefit from brighter dust emission.

Although there is some radial variation among molecular gas tracers from our observations, their overall spatial extent is similar, highlighting their utility for tracing molecular gas distribution. In real observations, one has to compromise the accuracy, availability, and brightness, making the choice of mid-J CO transitions more practical for these star-forming galaxies at cosmic noon.

6 The formation of massive star-forming galaxies

Our observations have provided a new, exquisite, deep view of the molecular gas distribution in ten massive MS galaxies at cosmic noon. We have analyzed the available multi-wavelength data, constraining their mass–size relation, bulge growth, and the molecular gas distribution. The remaining key question is how this evidence informs our understanding of the general evolution of massive star-forming galaxies around cosmic noon. In this section, we compare our new observations with existing studies of similarly gas-rich but compact starbursting galaxies to investigate how different gas accretion modes drive the evolution of massive galaxies.

6.1 The origin of the cold gas

Direct gas accretion is argued as the most common channel to support the growth of star-forming galaxies at cosmic noon (Genel et al., 2010; Somerville and Davé, 2015; Naab and Ostriker, 2017; Tacconi et al., 2020). Within this framework, the available sources of cold gas include gas-rich minor mergers, gas streams from the cosmic web, and cooling flows from recycled gas. Depending on the smoothness of gas accretion, this scenario predicts different consequences for global star-formation patterns and quenching (Dekel et al., 2009; Dekel and Burkert, 2014). With more steady gas accretion, the accreted gas first settles in the galactic disk and reaches a global equilibrium with the galactic integrated SFR. In contrast, more stochastic gas accretion–including gas-rich minor mergers–can be more chaotic, it could significantly increase the gas fraction of the galactic disk over a short timescale and enhance the disk instability(Genzel et al., 2008; Zolotov et al., 2015; Tacchella et al., 2016). In NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} galaxies, extended gas-rich disks are observed, consistent with feeding by steady gas accretion. The gas fraction of the disk is generally below 50 per cent, with a Toomre QQ stability parameter between 0.300.30–0.780.78 (75), indicating that these galaxies are not subject to the disruptive instability expected in the stochastic gas accretion or gas-rich mergers.

The halo properties of NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} galaxies also support the steady cold gas accretion. Based on the halo mass estimation (see §4.2), most NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} galaxies have halo mass around 0.8−6×1012​M⊙0.8-6\times 10^{12}\penalty\ \text{M}_{\odot}. According to Dekel and Birnboim (2006), halos of these masses lie close to the boundary of where cold accretion through cosmic web is still possible. Even without the direct cold accretion, the cooling flows from the hot halo can still support the growth of the stellar disk (van de Voort et al., 2011; Sultan et al., 2026, e.g.).

6.2 The transport of cold gas

Under the assumption of semi-steady gas accretion, accreted gas first settles in the outer galactic disk, which can extend up to ∼\sim10 kpc (Kereš et al., 2005; Dekel et al., 2009; Danovich et al., 2015), comparable to the extent of the observed molecular gas in NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} galaxies. To sustain global star formation, particularly the growth of the central bulge, the gas needs to be transported inward efficiently.

In systems with prominent galactic structures such as spiral arms and stellar bars, gravitational torques represent a widely discussed channel for radial gas flows (Pastras et al., 2026). Observational evidence of net gas inflow has been extensively reported in the nearby Universe (Wong et al., 2004; Davies et al., 2009; Sormani et al., 2023). The inferred net gas inflow rates range from 0.1–10 M⊙yr−1{}_{\odot}\text{yr}^{-1}, with velocities on the order of a few km s-1 (Schmidt et al., 2016; Di Teodoro and Peek, 2021; López-Cobá et al., 2025). The inflow rates, though often calculated with large uncertainties, are generally comparable to the ongoing star formation rates in these systems. Similar net inflows have also been reported in cosmological zoom-in simulations (Trapp et al., 2022, e.g.,).

At higher redshifts, galactic disks are generally more gas-rich and turbulent, potentially supporting stronger gas inflow rates. Prominent disk and bar structures were difficult to confirm in the HST era, where only rest-frame optical images were available for galaxies at cosmic noon. With the advent of JWST, we can now clearly identify and resolve these stellar structures. All the NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} galaxies show prominent spiral arms (see Figs. 1,2 and more clearly with the bulge and smooth disk removed in Fig. 3). A stellar bar is also visible in GN4_32842, G4_38232, and possibly in GN4_24517 and G4_17555. Similar spiral arms and bars have also been identified in galaxies up to z∼5z\sim 5 (Costantin et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2023; Le Conte et al., 2024; Tsukui et al., 2025; Espejo Salcedo et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025), highlighting that their role in driving gas flows may have begun much earlier in cosmic history. Observationally, Genzel et al. (2023) has shown evidence of gas radial flows in cosmic noon galaxies, in correspondence of bars and spiral arms. They reported radial flow velocities up to ∼\sim100 km s-1, almost an order of magnitude higher than in local galaxies. Pastras et al. (2025) also provided the first evidence of gas inflow in the barred galaxy GN4-32842, indicating rapid molecular gas inflow at a rate comparable to the ongoing SFR (Pastras et al., 2026, see also). 75 systematically analyzed radial gas flows in all NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} galaxies, finding that the ubuquitous presence of gas inflow and outflow, with a net gas inflow rate largely comparable to the integrated galactic SFR. The generally flat radial profiles of gas fraction and depletion time further support the view that net gas inflow and star formation have reached a local equilibrium within the disk, so there is no significant local gas accumulation or deficit.

6.3 Star-formation quenching

As the direct fuel of star formation, the spatial distribution of molecular gas is closely connected to star-formation and its quenching processes. In NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} galaxies, the comparable size between cold gas and stellar disk, as well as the flat molecular gas fraction and depletion timescale across the disks, support a balance between the local SFR and the available molecular gas. The resolved gas-depletion timescales in the center and outer disks are broadly similar to the integrated gas-depletion timescale of typical star-forming galaxies, which is on the order of 1 Gyr (Tacconi et al., 2020), indicating that these galaxies will not quench their star-forming activity on a timescale shorter than their dynamical timescale.

By comparison, the observed molecular gas in compact starburst galaxies at similar redshifts is mostly concentrated in the center with a much shorter depletion timescale of around 100 Myr (Tacconi et al., 2008; Dudzevičiūtė et al., 2020). Wet compaction provides a compelling framework for explaining their formation, in which dissipative compaction first leads to a highly concentrated molecular gas reservoir, triggering boosted star formation activity. This, in turn, quickly depletes the available cold gas, forming a dominant bulge component, and naturally explains the presence of compact, quenched galaxies at similar cosmic epochs (van Dokkum et al., 2008; Barro et al., 2013; Dekel and Burkert, 2014; Zolotov et al., 2015; Tacchella et al., 2016). Galaxies caught in the process of quenching their starburst core could have exhibited a ring-like molecular gas distribution around the central quenched core (Liu et al., 2023, e.g.).

For the quenching of the NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} galaxies, we therefore believe their halo will play a more important role during their secular evolution. The formation of the bulge component with steady gas transport could be delayed relative to that in compact starburst galaxies, weakening the bulge’s role in earlier quenching processes. Therefore, steady gas accretion may lead to the coexistence of a bulge component and ongoing star formation in the central region. As the entire galaxy grows, the halo mass will eventually play a leading role in quenching global star formation by preventing or slowing down cold gas accretion and recycling. With declining cold gas accretion, the galaxy will ultimately quench due to the depletion of available gas, but the disk morphology is more likely to be preserved. In the nearby Universe, as noted by Renzini (1999), there exists a mixed population of bulge-dominated systems, some with extended disks and some without. Without future disruptive merger processes, the NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} galaxies could be progenitors of quenched disk galaxies with less dominant bulge components, such as lenticular galaxies (Laurikainen et al., 2010; Saha and Cortesi, 2018; Moster et al., 2020), and possibly red spirals (Masters et al., 2010, e.g.).

Active galactic nuclei (AGN) could also play a distinct role in quenching, depending on the gas feeding conditions. During dissipative gas inflow, not only does the bulge grow rapidly, but so does the central supermassive black hole (SMBH), which may trigger strong AGN feedback shortly after bulge formation (Bluck et al., 2014; Genzel et al., 2014). This powerful AGN feedback can drive outflows that quickly remove available molecular gas or heat and ionize it (Fabian, 2012; King and Pounds, 2015). In cases of steady growth of the central bulge as we found for NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} galaxies, SMBH growth may lag behind that of the host galaxy (Ren et al., 2025), resulting in later and weaker AGN feedback. Future X-ray follow-up observations and spectral line diagnostics will provide more decisive tests of the importance of AGN in quenching star formation in these galaxies.

In Fig. 12, we illustrate the two different gas accretion scenarios by summarizing all their possible observational signatures. One notable difference between the two scenarios is the spatial distribution of molecular gas, dust, and stars. In the steady gas accretion scenario, these three components typically exhibit similar extents, and the galaxy will only wander gently around the canonical MS. In contrast, in stochastic gas accretion, galaxies exhibit more compact star-formation pattern traced by their compact dust emission. During this a stage, the galaxy can deviate significantly from the MS. It should be noted that there is likely no clear distinction between steady and stochastic gas accretion in the dynamic, complex galactic environment. Throughout the lifetime of a typical MS galaxy, both accretion modes could occur at different evolutionary stages.

Another line of observational evidence for secular evolution driven by steady gas accretion is the prevalence of massive, yet extended, disk galaxies in the early Universe. JWST has uncovered multiple giant disk galaxies (ReR_{\rm e} > 3 kpc) at z>1z>1 (Fudamoto et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2025; Umehata et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2025; Übler et al., 2024). In these systems, disks and bar-like structures are commonly observed, but exhibit a less dominant central bulge, features that align with steady gas accretion being the primary driver of their evolution. Jiang et al. (2025) systematically analyzed these “bulge-less” disk galaxies in the TNG simulation, supporting the idea that these galaxies reside in mildly overdense environments, which feature steady gas supply along cosmic filaments while avoiding disruptive merger events during their evolution.

Overall, depending on the dominance of these two different accretion modes, galaxies can evolve into different morphologies by the end of their star formation.

7 Conclusions

In this work, we studied the spatial distribution of molecular gas, traced by CO(3-2)/CO(4-3), [C i], and dust continuum from the NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} survey. We analyzed the size, radial profiles, and spatial distributions of different galactic components by combining NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} data with existing multi-band images. The main conclusions are as follows:

  1. 1.

    The deep, wideband NOEMA observations reveal a widely presence of extended cold molecular gas and dust in main-sequence galaxies at cosmic noon. Their sizes are largely comparable to those of the stellar disks, in contrast to the size differences observed in more compact dusty star-forming galaxies.

  2. 2.

    All NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} galaxies exhibit a prominent central stellar concentration in the rest-frame near-IR broadband images. Although they resemble the bulge component in more nearby galaxies, our bulge–disk decomposition generally supports that they are less dominant in mass, contributing to less than 25 per cent of the total mass of the host galaxy. They also show a generally lower Sérsic index than classical bulges.

  3. 3.

    Different molecular gas tracers are generally consistent with one another when observed at comparable sensitivities. In massive star-forming galaxies, the mid-J CO transition, such as CO(3-2) and CO(4-3), is generally brighter than other tracers at similar frequencies, and thus remains the best tracer for mapping the spatial distribution and kinematics of molecular gas. With the implementation of ultra-wide bandwidth in modern interferometers, dust continuum is becoming another promising tool.

  4. 4.

    The spatially resolved CO(4–3), [C i](1-0), and dust continuum generally follow the galactic integrated correlations, but show roughly two times larger scatter. The increased scatter indicates that ISM conditions begin to deviate from the globally averaged conditions already on scales of 3-6 kpc. This is consistent with the idea that the ISM in these star-forming galaxies is not well mixed on kpc scales, possibly reflecting ongoing gas accretion and clumpy star formation.

  5. 5.

    The resolved molecular gas fraction and molecular gas depletion timescale generally show a mild radial variation in most of these extended MS galaxies at cosmic noon, and it is largely consistent with their galactic integrated ones. It indicates that steady gas accretion and radial gas transport are supporting the buildup of extended disk galaxies, in contrast to the stochastic, clumpier gas accretion with wet compaction observed in compact starbursting galaxies at a similar cosmic time. Moreover, due to the less dominant bulge component, these extended disk galaxies will likely be quenched by the halo at a later time.

We highlight the crucial role of increased bandwidth and long baselines provided by NOEMA for such a large survey. The ongoing dual-band implementation will enable simultaneous sampling of multiple molecular lines to constrain their excitation temperatures and of multi-band dust emission to model the dust SED, making it even more efficient to fully map the ISM properties of galaxies across cosmic time. The more sensitive ALMA is also allocating significant time to these cosmic noon MS galaxies and is already on its way to implementing a bandwidth upgrade (Carpenter et al., 2023). These efforts will provide a significantly larger sample to fully understand the formation and evolution of typical massive disk galaxies since cosmic noon.

Appendix A Size comparison between the curve of growth and the Sérsic fitting

We first measured the size based on the reddest broadband filter whenever available. For the majority of our targets, F444W probes the rest-frame 2 μ\mum stellar continuum, which is much less affected by dust attenuation. One of our targets, G4-38065, does not have available JWST observations, so we used the reddest HST filter, F160W. For those targets with both JWST/F444W and HST/F160W observations, we found that F160W generally yields a larger size. We first fit the stellar emission with a PSF-convolved 2D Sérsic profile. Such fitting can greatly reduce the PSF blurring in the central region. The fitted Sérsic index is typically larger than that of a pure exponential disk profile (n = 1), indicating the presence of a central bulge in the majority of our targets.

From the residuals, we found that most of the 2D parametric Sérsic models leave extended disk structures, such as spiral arms. Considering the ubiquitous disk residuals after the 2D Sérsic fitting, we also applied the curve-of-growth method to measure the size of the stellar component. We first applied a single 2D Gaussian fit to determine the axis ratio and central position, then used elliptical apertures with the fixed axis ratio from the 2D Gaussian fit. We adopted the radius at which the enclosed broadband flux reaches half of its total value.

Generally, we found that both methods give comparable results. The 2D Sérsic fitting yields slightly smaller sizes than the curve-of-growth method, but the difference is usually smaller than the typical uncertainties of the measured size. The angular sizes of our targets are >>0.4 arcsec, which is larger than the typical FWHM of JWST/F444W and HST/F160W. Also considering the ubiquitous presence of extended disk structures (which are less affected by PSF blurring), we adopt the curve-of-growth results as the final stellar size.

Appendix B Dust temperature

Dust temperatures vary across galaxies, typically being higher near star-forming regions. To test how much varying dust temperature profiles affect final size measurements, we measured the sizes of an ideal galaxy with different temperature profiles. We parameterized the dust radial temperature as exponential profile Tdust​(r)∝r−αT_{\text{dust}}(r)\propto r^{-\alpha}. The galaxy was constructed with a 2D Sérsic profile with n=1n=1 to approximate the general extended disk morphology of the NOEMA3D{}^{\text{3D}} galaxies. We find that steeper temperature profiles predict larger disk sizes, indicating that the constant-temperature assumption tends to underestimate the true size of the dust distribution. However, the overall effect is generally small; even with a steep slope of 0.4, the size difference remains within 0.3 dex, typically smaller than the measured uncertainties. Due to the lack of observational constraints on the temperature gradient of cosmic noon galaxies, we did not apply corrections for it. Nevertheless, the generally underestimated dust size does not change the conclusions of our work.

Appendix C UV modeling

The visibility fitting results for all targets are presented in Appendix Fig. 15 and 16 for the group-1 targets, and Fig. 17 for the group-2 targets. For each individual system, only the converged fits are shown. The best-fit parameters for each target are provided in Table 4. Parameters without error bars were held fixed during the fitting process.

Appendix D Morphological analysis

We applied a morphological analysis based on statmorph to the cold ISM maps from CO, [C I], and dust continuum. The results are shown in Fig. D. For most metrics, the measurements across different tracers scatter around the one-to-one correlation. The strongest deviation from the one-to-one correlation is seen in M20 between CO and [C I], where CO exhibits a systematic larger M20 value, indicating that CO emission is more spreaded than [C I]. This appears contradictory to the general consensus that [C I] traces more diffuse molecular gas than CO. However, given the limited sample size and the small magnitude of the offset, a larger sample with improved statistics is needed to better quantify their morphological differences.

Appendix E Radial gas fraction and depletion timescale

We calculated the radial gas mass profile using all three cold gas tracers, which allowed us to independently derive the radial gas fraction and depletion timescale. The results from the different tracers are shown in Fig. 19. As noted in the main text, there is considerable scatter from galaxy to galaxy, but most exhibit only moderate radial variation. The sample-averaged radial profile also shows a generally flat trend.
